topic: Phrasal Verbs for Work, Ideas and Problems

scenarios.scenario: Coming up with a new plan
scenarios.context: Two colleagues plan a campaign to reduce waste in their office.

speakerA.en: Our manager wants us to come up with a way of cutting paper use by half. Have you got any ideas?
That sounds promising, but would people actually go along with it? Some of them hate change.
Good thinking. Shall I put the proposal forward at Monday's meeting?
I'll draw up a short report with the costs. Could you look it over before I send it?
I won't. I'll have it ready by Thursday, so you'll have time to go through it.
That would be great. Imagine how much waste we'd cut down on across the whole company.

speakerB.en: I've been looking into it. We could set up a shared digital system, so nobody needs to print documents out.
Most will once they see the benefits. We could carry out a small trial in one department before rolling it out to everyone.
Yes, but make sure you point out the savings. Figures tend to win people over.
Of course. Just don't leave it until the last minute, because I'm snowed under with work this week.
Perfect. If the idea takes off, we could even help other offices set up the same system.
Let's not get carried away. First we have to win over the sceptics.

scenarios.scenario: Coping with a problem at work
scenarios.context: A team leader and a colleague deal with a server failure before an important deadline.

speakerA.en: The system broke down again this morning, and we've fallen behind on the report. What are we going to do?
The technician says the data wasn't backed up, so we may have to start over.
I'll ask the other team whether anyone can step in. They owe us a favour anyway.
Won't that make us look unprofessional? I'd rather we tried to pull it off without telling them.
You're right. It's better than letting them down at the last minute.
Agreed. I'll set up automatic backups first thing tomorrow.

speakerB.en: Stay calm. First, let's find out what went wrong, and then we can sort it out step by step.
That's a disaster. We'll have to take on extra help if we want to make up for the lost time.
Good idea. Meanwhile, I'll ring the client and explain that we might not be able to hand the report in on time.
I'd rather be honest. Clients usually put up with a short delay if you warn them in advance.
Exactly. Once this is over, we need to work out how to stop it from happening again.
Brilliant. Let's get on with it, and hopefully we'll get through the rest of today without further trouble.

scenarios.context: Members of a student committee argue about how to spend their budget.

speakerA.en: I'd like to bring up the budget for the end-of-year party. I think we're spending far too much.
I'm not suggesting we do away with it, only that we find a cheaper venue.
Then what about asking local businesses to chip in? Some of them have sponsored events before.
True. I'll talk to the cafe on the corner and see whether they'll come round to the idea.
Maybe, as long as we can liven it up with decorations and a good playlist.
Understood. Let's put it to a vote and abide by the result.

speakerB.en: I see where you're coming from, but a good party brings people together. We shouldn't cut back on it too much.
I'm afraid I can't go along with that. The school hall is boring, and nobody will turn up.
It's worth a try. I'd rule out the cinema, though. They turned us down last year.
And if they refuse, will you back down and accept the hall?
That's a fair compromise. I won't give in on the food, though. That needs a proper budget.
Agreed. It's better than falling out over a party.

scenarios.scenario: Money and keeping a business going
scenarios.context: A shop owner talks to her accountant about a difficult year.

speakerA.en: Business has been slow, and we've almost run out of savings. I'm not sure how much longer we can carry on.
We've already cut back on staff hours. I don't want to lay anyone off.
Just about, but I've had to put off buying new stock, and that's hurting sales.
I'd love to, but there's hardly anything left over. Our main competitor has taken over half of our customers.
I've looked into it, but I don't know where to start.
That would be wonderful. I don't want to give up after all these years.

speakerB.en: Let's go through the figures. The first step is to cut down on costs that aren't essential.
Understandable. What about the loan? Are you managing to pay it off every month?
Then consider setting aside a small amount each week, so you don't get caught out again.
Then you need to stand out. Have you thought about selling online? It could bring in new customers.
I can put you in touch with someone who set up a similar business last year. She might be able to help out.
You won't have to. With a few changes, I think you can turn things around.

scenarios.context: Two old friends talk about family, forgiveness and moving on.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about my brother. We fell out years ago, and I still haven't got over it.
I'm afraid he'll turn me down. I let him down badly when he needed me.
You're probably right. I do look up to him. He's always been the one I could count on.
How did you manage? Did you bring it up straight away?
That gives me hope. I'm tired of putting up with this silence.
I'll write to him tonight. Thanks for talking me round.

speakerB.en: That's hard. Have you tried getting in touch with him? Sometimes people are waiting for the other person to make the first move.
People can forgive a lot if you own up to your mistakes. Apologise, and try to make up for it.
Then tell him that. In my family, we grew apart for a while after my parents split up, but we sorted it out.
No, I put it off for months. When I finally did, I found out that he had been feeling the same way.
Then don't wait. The longer you leave it, the harder it becomes to face up to.
Any time. And let me know how it turns out. I'll be rooting for you.
